summary: This program keeps a travel packing list in an ArrayList of strings, prints it as a numbered list, then adds one item and removes another before printing the updated list. It shows that a List allows duplicate values and that removing by name only takes out the first match.

lines.text: ArrayList is the concrete list implementation supplied by the Java library, and it must be imported before it can be used.
List is the interface that describes what any list can do, so importing both lets you declare the variable as a List while building an ArrayList.

The variable is typed as List but holds an ArrayList, a common Java habit that keeps the code tied to the general behaviour rather than one implementation. The <String> says every element is a string.
add appends an element to the end of the list, so the order in which you call it is the order the items keep.
A List happily stores the same value twice, which is exactly what you want for a packing list holding two pairs of socks.
size() reports how many elements the list currently holds, and because list positions start at 0 the loop must stop before that number.
get(i) fetches the element at position i, and printing i + 1 turns the zero-based index into the 1, 2, 3 numbering a reader expects.
The \n escape starts a blank line before the message, which separates the two printed lists visually.
Passing a string to remove deletes the first element equal to it and leaves the second "Socks" in place, so a duplicate needs a second call to disappear entirely.
